romanticism: Imagine being alive when trains were replacing horse-drawn transportation, factories were growing, and people were fighting over what freedom should mean. The nineteenth century was a time when ordinary life was changing faster than many people could understand. Some welcomed progress, while others worried about what society was losing. Artists and writers tried to make sense of those changes by showing not only what happened, but also how people felt about it. My main point is that nineteenth-century politics, Romantic art, social criticism, and industrial inventions changed how people understood freedom and progress, and they still influence the world I am preparing to work in.

The century began in the shadow of the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars, which changed governments and borders across Europe. After Napoleon’s defeat in 1815, rulers tried to restore stability, but demands for political rights and national independence did not disappear. Revolutions broke out in several European countries in 1848, and nationalism helped lead to the unification of Italy and Germany later in the century. European empires also expanded overseas, often with terrible consequences for colonized populations. Life depended a lot on geography and social class: cities grew around factories and trade, while many rural communities still depended on farming. Religion remained important, even as scientific ideas and new political movements challenged older assumptions.

Romanticism was one way people responded to this uncertain world. It developed in literature, music, and painting, especially in Europe, and placed strong value on imagination, nature, individuality, and emotion. Instead of always presenting calm, idealized heroes, Romantic artists could show terror, loneliness, beauty, or a person struggling against something much bigger than themselves. Writers such as William Wordsworth and Victor Hugo explored human feelings and injustice, while composers used dramatic contrasts and expressive melodies. In paintings by Géricault and Turner, nature can feel both magnificent and dangerous. I find that interesting because these artists seemed willing to admit that human beings do not control everything, even during an age that celebrated human progress.

This period also produced powerful criticism of social inequality. Nationalism inspired people who wanted independence or a shared identity, but it could also create conflict and exclusion. Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, published in 1862, uses characters such as Jean Valjean to explore poverty, punishment, mercy, and the treatment of vulnerable people. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto in 1848, arguing that conflict between social classes shaped industrial society. Their proposals were very different from Hugo’s novel, but both works asked readers to pay attention to people who were often overlooked. Painters such as Jean-François Millet did something similar by treating farm laborers as worthy subjects for serious art. All of this makes the century feel less distant to me, because arguments about fairness, work, and opportunity are still around.

The Industrial Revolution may be the part of the nineteenth century that most directly connects to my future. Steam power, machinery, railroads, and later electrical technologies helped businesses produce goods and connect communities at a much larger scale. Those changes also created dangerous jobs, pollution, and unequal working conditions. As a software engineering student who wants to build useful businesses, I can see a direct connection between those inventions and what programmers do today. A factory machine automated physical work; software now automates information, scheduling, communication, and many everyday decisions. That does not mean every new technology is automatically good. I want to build products that genuinely help people, and this history reminds me that efficiency matters, but so do the people affected by what we create.
impressionism: A painting that looks unfinished up close can become surprisingly beautiful when you stand a few steps away. That is one of the things I like about Impressionism: it asks the viewer to see an ordinary moment differently. By the second half of the nineteenth century, European cities were changing because of industry, transportation, photography, and new ways of spending free time. Artists began questioning why they had to paint exactly as academic institutions expected. My main point is that Impressionism grew out of modern urban life and changed art by making light, everyday experience, and personal observation more important than perfectly polished detail.

France, especially Paris, became the center of Impressionism. Under Napoleon III, Paris was dramatically rebuilt with broad streets and new public spaces, while trains made travel to nearby towns and the countryside easier. Cafés, parks, theaters, and dance gardens gave artists new scenes to paint. At the same time, the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 and the Paris Commune showed that social and political instability had not disappeared. Many artists were frustrated with the official Salon, whose juries controlled much of the art world. In 1874, a group including Claude Monet and Edgar Degas organized an independent exhibition. Their work was criticized for looking sketchy, but the exhibition became a major turning point in modern art.

Impressionist painters were interested in what the eye notices in a particular moment. Monet studied reflections, weather, and the way sunlight changes colors; Renoir painted people enjoying social activities; and Degas often focused on dancers and urban interiors. They used visible brushstrokes, brighter colors, and unusual compositions instead of hiding every mark of the brush. Painting outdoors became especially important for landscapes, although Impressionists also worked in studios. Photography was another influence because it encouraged cropped scenes and unexpected viewpoints. What I like about this approach is that the artists did not always need a dramatic historical event to make something meaningful. Even a harbor at sunrise or friends dancing could become a subject worth remembering.

Impressionism also says something about society in the late nineteenth century. Its scenes of leisure reflect a growing urban middle class, but they do not represent everyone’s experience. Factory workers and poorer families often lived very different lives from the people attending fashionable cafés and dances. Women artists, including Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt, contributed important perspectives even though their access to public spaces and professional opportunities was more restricted. Later artists took Impressionist experiments in new directions: van Gogh used color and brushwork to communicate powerful feelings, while Edvard Munch made anxiety itself a major subject. These artists are usually classified as Post-Impressionist or Symbolist rather than simply Impressionist. Together they show that art was moving away from one accepted definition of beauty.

The technology of this era also connects to software engineering and entrepreneurship. Railroads helped people reach new places, industrial manufacturing made materials more available, and photography changed how images could be created and shared. In a different way, digital tools now make it easier for someone to design, publish, and build a business without needing approval from a traditional institution. The Impressionists remind me of small teams who try something different even when established organizations do not take them seriously at first. I do not think being different is enough by itself; the work still has to offer real value. But their example encourages me to experiment, learn from criticism, and keep improving an idea instead of assuming that the usual way is the only possible way.
artworks: Théodore Géricault — The Raft of the Medusa (1818–1819)

Géricault’s The Raft of the Medusa is a huge oil painting on canvas based on a real French shipwreck. Survivors were abandoned on a makeshift raft, and the disaster became a political scandal. In the painting, some people are dead or exhausted while others desperately signal toward a distant ship. The diagonal arrangement of bodies makes the scene feel like it is moving from hopelessness toward one last chance of rescue. Its enormous size was unusual for a contemporary tragedy instead of a traditional heroic story. I think its strongest message is that human suffering deserves to be seen, even when it makes the government or the viewer uncomfortable. This is a defining Romantic work because of its intense emotion, dramatic nature, and willingness to criticize the world around it.
J. M. W. Turner — The Fighting Temeraire (1839)

Turner’s The Fighting Temeraire is an oil painting on canvas showing an old British warship being pulled by a small steam-powered tugboat. The Temeraire had fought at Trafalgar, but in the painting it is being taken away to be dismantled. Turner makes the old ship glow almost like a ghost, while the tugboat looks dark and mechanical. The dramatic sunset suggests that an entire era is ending, not just the life of one ship. It is especially interesting that the steam engine represents the new Industrial Revolution while the sailing ship represents the past. Rather than painting an exact historical record, Turner used color and atmosphere to express loss and change. This combination of history, emotion, and symbolism makes the work an excellent example of Romanticism.

Millet’s The Gleaners is an oil painting on canvas that shows three poor women gathering leftover grain after the harvest. The workers are bent over, repeating a tiring movement, while larger piles of harvested crops appear in the background. That contrast makes the difference between agricultural wealth and poverty easy to notice. The painting is associated with Realism, which focused on ordinary people and everyday conditions rather than idealized heroes. Some contemporary viewers found its attention to rural poverty politically uncomfortable. I appreciate how Millet gives the women dignity without pretending their work is easy or glamorous. The scene is important because it shows that social class and labor could be serious subjects for art.

Monet’s Impression, Sunrise is an oil painting on canvas showing the harbor at Le Havre in the early morning. Instead of describing every boat and building in sharp detail, Monet uses loose brushstrokes, gray-blue mist, and a small bright orange sun. The reflection on the water matters as much as the physical objects. When it appeared in the 1874 independent exhibition, a critic used the title to mock the new style, and the name Impressionism became associated with the movement. I like that the painting captures a brief experience rather than trying to make the harbor look permanent. It is a typical Impressionist work because light, color, atmosphere, and the feeling of a particular moment are more important than perfect outlines.
Pierre-Auguste Renoir — Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876)

Renoir’s Dance at the Moulin de la Galette is an oil painting on canvas of people gathering at a lively outdoor dance spot in Montmartre, Paris. The scene includes conversations, dancing, fashionable clothing, and sunlight filtering through the trees. Renoir uses quick, colorful brushstrokes so the crowd almost seems to be moving. The painting was shown at an Impressionist exhibition in 1877, and its loose appearance drew criticism from some viewers. To me, its meaning is not about one famous person or important battle; it is about the experience of being together and enjoying an ordinary afternoon. It reflects the growing leisure culture of modern Paris and the Impressionist interest in everyday life and shifting light.
Vincent van Gogh — The Starry Night (1889)

Van Gogh’s The Starry Night is an oil painting on canvas, created while he was staying at Saint-Rémy in France. The sky is filled with swirling lines, bright stars, and a moon above a quiet village. A dark cypress tree rises in the foreground, connecting the land and sky. Although the painting was inspired by a real view, van Gogh changed it to express an emotional, almost dreamlike experience. The contrast between the calm village and the moving sky makes the painting feel both peaceful and unsettled to me. This is better described as Post-Impressionism because van Gogh pushed beyond recording visible light and used bold color and brushwork to communicate feeling. It helped open the way for more expressive modern art.

Munch’s The Scream is a work on cardboard made with tempera and crayon in the well-known 1893 painted version. A figure stands on a bridge holding its face while the sky and landscape twist into intense waves of color. The two people farther away seem disconnected from the person in the foreground. Instead of showing a realistic portrait, Munch turns the entire environment into an expression of fear or anxiety. The figure almost seems to hear or feel the scream of nature itself. I find it memorable because the emotion is immediately understandable even without knowing the artist’s story. The work belongs more closely to Symbolism and the beginnings of Expressionism than to Impressionism, showing how late-nineteenth-century art increasingly explored the inner mind.
music: Schubert’s Erlkönig is a German art song, or Lied, for solo voice and piano, based on a poem by Goethe. The story follows a father carrying his sick child through the night while the child believes a threatening supernatural figure is pursuing him. The rapid repeated piano notes suggest the urgency of the horse’s gallop, while the singer changes expression to portray the narrator, father, son, and Erlking. The music shifts in dynamics and harmony as the child becomes more frightened, creating a scene that feels almost like a small opera. The words are essential because the music responds to the events and feelings in the poem. Its frightening atmosphere and focus on the supernatural make it a strong example of Romantic music.
Richard Wagner — Ride of the Valkyries (Die Walküre, 1870)

Ride of the Valkyries is an orchestral and vocal scene that opens Act III of Wagner’s opera Die Walküre, part of the Ring cycle. The Valkyries are mythological figures who carry fallen warriors from battle, and the music makes their flight sound powerful and exciting. The fast-moving accompaniment, bold brass melody, and strong rhythms give it a sense of motion and force. The dynamics are often loud and dramatic, with layers of instruments creating a thick orchestral texture. Wagner also used recurring musical ideas, or leitmotifs, to connect music with characters and events in his operas. This scene represents Romanticism through its mythology, enormous emotional scale, and close connection between the story and the sound.
Hector Berlioz — March to the Scaffold (Symphonie fantastique, 1830)

March to the Scaffold is the fourth movement of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, a program symphony that tells the story of an artist’s disturbing dream. In this episode, the artist imagines he is being marched toward execution. The steady march rhythm and heavy brass and percussion make the music feel threatening, while sudden changes in volume keep it unpredictable. Near the end, a brief return of the melody representing his beloved is interrupted by a sharp orchestral gesture suggesting the execution. This recurring melody, called the idée fixe, helps connect the whole symphony. I find the movement unusually visual because it feels like the orchestra is narrating a movie scene without words. Its dramatic storytelling is a classic Romantic feature.
Frédéric Chopin — Polonaise in A-flat Major, Op. 53, “Heroic” (1842)

Chopin’s Heroic Polonaise is a solo piano piece based on the rhythm of a traditional Polish dance. It begins with a bold, brilliant character and builds through strong chords, energetic rhythms, and demanding passages. The famous repeated octaves in the middle create a powerful, almost military feeling, although the piece also includes more lyrical moments. Because Chopin lived away from Poland during a period when his homeland lacked political independence, the polonaise could carry a strong sense of national identity. The title “Heroic” reflects the proud, confident mood associated with the work. Its mix of virtuoso piano writing, emotion, and nationalism makes it especially representative of Romantic music.
Claude Debussy — Clair de lune (Suite bergamasque, published 1905)

Clair de lune is a solo piano piece by Debussy and the third movement of his Suite bergamasque. Although the suite was published in 1905, its roots go back to the late nineteenth century, so it connects well with the transition into musical modernism. The piece begins softly with a gentle, spacious melody and changes in tempo, dynamics, and flowing texture. Rather than telling a clear story, it suggests moonlight through delicate harmonies and a dreamy atmosphere. Some passages become fuller and more intense before the music returns to a quiet ending. I like the way it creates a specific feeling without needing lyrics. Debussy is often connected to musical Impressionism, although that label does not completely describe his style.
